turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor, vitals are in. Blood pressure is 128 over 82, heart rate 76, oxygen sat 98 percent. He didn't say much out in the waiting room.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, I'll take it from here. Mr. Hale, I'm Dr. Shah. What brought you in today?
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll jump in, if that's allowed. I'm June, his partner, I live with him. He's not been himself since his father died and he got laid off.
[SEG0004] person_4 (PATIENT): I'm fine, Doctor. Truly. I don't wish to make a fuss.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): I hear you, and I appreciate how you're putting it. June is the one who asked for the visit, though, so I'd like her account and then yours.

[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sleep is a mess. He's up most of the night, maybe three or four hours total, and there's no energy to speak of. He stopped the model trains completely. He pushes the plate away, and this has been, um, five months, since his dad passed in March.
[SEG0007] person_4 (PATIENT): If I may, that is not quite accurate. I do eat, I had oatmeal this morning, and I still look at the trains. I am not entirely without interest.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): All right. So from your side the appetite is fine, and the interest is dulled, not gone. How long has the sleep actually been poor, in your own words?
[SEG0009] person_4 (PATIENT): Well, actually, closer to three months. After the funeral I was managing. It slipped, um, sometime after that.
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I don't know. It felt like right from the funeral to me, so five months. Maybe I'm bundling the whole awful stretch together.

[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me think this through out loud. I'm hearing three months from you and about five from June, and I can't pin a start date either of you is sure of. I'll hold it as roughly three to five months.
[SEG0012] person_4 (PATIENT): That seems fair. I apologize for the muddle.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): No apology needed. Walk me through a typical night.
[SEG0014] person_4 (PATIENT): I get into bed near eleven. I may doze after midnight, then I am awake around three and I do not really get back to sleep. I am tired all the next day.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And then he naps in the armchair after lunch, which I swear makes the night worse. Also the dog's been stealing his pillow, but that's, well, not why we're here.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the dog out of the chart. Is that low energy there most days, Mr. Hale?
[SEG0017] person_4 (PATIENT): Yes. Most days. I stay polite about it at home, but it is wearying.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the interest, if we drop the word completely?
[SEG0019] person_4 (PATIENT): I said I was fine, and that was not the whole truth. I have lost interest in the workshop. I still read the paper. I am not indifferent to every single thing.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He also won't see people. His friend called twice and he just let it ring.
[SEG0021] person_4 (PATIENT): I did see Robert last Sunday, briefly. I would not say that I will not see anyone.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): One visit isn't the old social calendar, but I won't inflate it. Do you feel hopeless about the weeks ahead?
[SEG0023] person_4 (PATIENT): Flat, I would say. Not hopeless. I still expect the days to keep coming.

[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I need to ask something I ask anyone when energy and interest fall off like this, and I'll ask it gently. Have you had thoughts of hurting yourself, or of not wanting to be here?
[SEG0025] person_4 (PATIENT): No. I have not. I want to be quite clear that I have no thoughts of harming myself.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. I believe you. Any chest pain, or trouble getting your breath, along with the fatigue?
[SEG0027] person_4 (PATIENT): No chest pain. And no shortness of breath.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you taking any medicines on a regular basis?
[SEG0029] person_4 (PATIENT): Nothing regularly. I would prefer to keep it that way, if possible.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies, to a medicine or to anything else?
[SEG0031] person_4 (PATIENT): None that I am aware of.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sometimes low energy is a blood test and not just the mood. Did anyone ever check your thyroid, or say you were anemic?
[SEG0033] person_4 (PATIENT): Two years ago my previous physician ordered a thyroid test. They said it was borderline. I was never started on a medicine for it, and I do not have the number.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Borderline, and no value in front of us. I'm not going to treat a result we can't see. I'd like to repeat the thyroid blood test so we stop guessing.
[SEG0035] person_4 (PATIENT): Yes. That would be acceptable.
[SEG0036] person_3 (CAREGIVER): His father died of a heart attack, if you need that. And Daniel was laid off from the bookkeeping job in April, so he's home all day.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Useful, thank you. Mr. Hale, do you smoke, or drink alcohol?
[SEG0038] person_4 (PATIENT): I do not smoke. I might have a small glass of wine on a Sunday, and nothing more than that.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Looking you over, you're well groomed, your speech is clear, and I don't see a tremor in the hands. You do look tired. Nothing acute is jumping out on this quick exam.

[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thinking out loud, this looks like a depressive episode, and I mean a working impression rather than a final label, with the grief and the job loss underneath it. The poor sleep, the low energy, and the thinner interest all fit. I also can't fully rule out a thyroid contribution, given that old borderline test, so that stays on the differential until the lab speaks.
[SEG0041] person_4 (PATIENT): I understand. I would rather not begin a medicine today, if you feel that is reasonable.

[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): It is reasonable, and I won't start one today. If you're still this low when I see you in four weeks, we could start sertraline at fifty milligrams. We can decide that then, not in this room.

[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Between now and then, the useful steps are ordinary ones. Pick a single wake-up time and keep it, even after a bad night, and skip the long nap after lunch. If any thought of harming yourself shows up, you call the office or you go to the emergency room, and you do not wait the four weeks.
[SEG0044] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll help him with the wake-up time. Sorry, the parking garage took twenty minutes off my temper, which is not relevant, I know.

[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm putting in a referral to our behavioral health counselor, so the two of you aren't carrying this alone. The thyroid blood draw can happen today if the nurse is still around.
[SEG0046] person_1 (NURSE): I can walk him to the lab once you're finished. We're still drawing for a bit.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Mr. Hale, I want to see you in four weeks either way, not only if you feel worse. We'll look at the thyroid and only then talk about whether sertraline makes sense.
[SEG0048] person_4 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate the care you have taken with this.

test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

omissions.text: Regular medications: patient said he takes nothing regularly and would prefer to keep it that way if possible.
Sleep details: goes to bed near 11, may doze after midnight, wakes around 3 AM, and does not really get back to sleep; tired all the next day.
Daytime napping after lunch was reported by the caregiver.

Appetite/loss of interest were characterized differently by the patient: appetite described as fine/eating, and interest as dulled not gone; he still looks at the trains and reads the paper, and is not indifferent to every single thing.
